title: Equality, diversity and challenging discrimination
blurb: Name the nine protected characteristics, spot each type of discrimination, make reasonable adjustments and challenge discriminatory behaviour.
question: A ward policy says all patients must complete a written menu card by 10am or receive a standard meal. A patient with a visual impairment keeps missing out on her choice. What does the law require of the ward?

teach.h: Equality is not treating everyone the same
teach.body: Equality means everyone has a fair chance of the same outcome. Sometimes that needs different treatment, such as a large-print menu or extra time. The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination because of nine protected characteristics. The Code requires you to treat people fairly and without discrimination, bullying or harassment (20.2), to avoid assumptions and recognise diversity (1.3), and to challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour relating to care (3.4).

teach.caption: Marriage and civil partnership is not one of the characteristics covered by the public sector equality duty (s149(7)).

head: Type
Meaning
rows: Less favourable treatment because of a characteristic
A rule for everyone that disadvantages a group
Unfavourable treatment because of something linked to disability
Unwanted conduct that violates dignity or is hostile
Detriment for complaining or helping a complaint

teach.body: Where a disabled person is put at a substantial disadvantage, there is a duty to take reasonable steps to avoid it. There are three requirements: change a provision, criterion or practice; change or avoid a physical feature; and provide an auxiliary aid. Where information is involved, reasonable steps include providing it in an accessible format. The disabled person cannot be charged for the adjustment.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Sofia on an orthopaedic ward
teach.body: Ms Begum, 67, who has a visual impairment, keeps getting a standard meal because she cannot read the menu card by 10am. The rule applies to everyone, but it puts her at a substantial disadvantage because of her disability. Sofia reads the menu to her each morning and requests a large-print card: a reasonable adjustment to a practice and an auxiliary aid. She records the need so the next shift continues it.

teach.caption: Public authorities such as NHS trusts must have due regard to these three aims in everything they do.

items: Unconscious bias: automatic assumptions about people that we are not aware of. Recognise your own (Annexe A 1.7).
Check assumptions about pain, capacity or wishes based on age, race, disability or appearance.
If you see discriminatory behaviour, challenge it calmly and promptly, and support the person affected.
Report it through local policy, and escalate if it continues.

teach.text: INDIRECT discrimination is the same rule for everyone that hits one group harder (a written-only menu, a no-headwear rule). DIRECT discrimination is treating someone worse BECAUSE of a characteristic. Don't mix them up.

items: Nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.
s20: reasonable adjustments to practices, physical features and auxiliary aids, in accessible formats, at no cost to the person.
s149: eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity, foster good relations.
Code 3.4 and 20.2: treat people fairly and challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour.

summary: You can now list the nine protected characteristics and tell direct, indirect and disability-related discrimination, harassment and victimisation apart. You can also make reasonable adjustments and explain how to challenge discrimination in practice.

A.q: Which of these is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
A.why: Section 4 lists nine protected characteristics, including pregnancy and maternity.

whyNot.1: Socio-economic status is not one of the nine protected characteristics.
whyNot.2: Political affiliation is not listed as a protected characteristic in s4.
whyNot.3: Body mass index is not itself a protected characteristic.

A.q: A healthcare assistant refuses to help a patient wash because the patient is gay. Which type of discrimination is this?
A.why: Direct discrimination (s13) is treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic, here sexual orientation.

whyNot.0: Indirect discrimination is a neutral rule that disadvantages a group; this is personal, targeted treatment.
whyNot.1: Victimisation is detriment for making or supporting a complaint.
whyNot.3: Failure to make reasonable adjustments relates to disability.

A.q: Which is one of the three aims of the public sector equality duty?
options: Promote the use of private care
A.why: Section 149 requires due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity and fostering good relations.

whyNot.0: Promoting private care is not part of s149.
whyNot.1: Waiting times are an NHS target, not a s149 aim.
whyNot.2: s149 does not set recruitment quotas.

B.q: A clinic sends all appointment letters in standard print. A patient who is blind misses appointments as a result. What type of duty is engaged?
options: The duty to make reasonable adjustments
The duty of confidentiality to patients
The duty to safeguard adults at risk
B.why: A practice puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage, so s20 requires reasonable steps, including information in an accessible format.

whyNot.0: Candour concerns openness when care goes wrong.
whyNot.2: Confidentiality is about protecting information, not access to it.
whyNot.3: This is not abuse or neglect requiring safeguarding.

B.q: A trust changes a patient's bathroom to fit grab rails so she can use it after her stroke. Which s20 requirement does this meet?
B.why: The second requirement of s20 concerns physical features that put a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage.

whyNot.0: Auxiliary aids are items or services such as hearing loops or interpreters, not building changes.
whyNot.1: Criteria are rules, not the physical layout.
whyNot.2: Practices are ways of working, not physical features.

B.q: A patient makes racist comments to a student nurse while she is caring for him. What is the most appropriate action for the registered nurse?
options: Move the student to another bay and carry on
Laugh it off to calm the situation
Challenge it, support the student and report it
Note it and discuss it at the next team meeting
B.why: The Code requires nurses to treat people without discrimination or harassment (20.2) and to challenge discriminatory behaviour. Supporting the student and reporting through local policy are part of this.

whyNot.0: Moving the student avoids the behaviour without challenging it or supporting her.
whyNot.1: Laughing it off condones the behaviour.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a meeting delays support for the student.

C.q: A ward rule states that patients may not use their phones after 9pm. A deaf patient relies on text messaging to communicate with her family. What is the most accurate analysis?
options: The rule may put her at a disadvantage requiring an adjustment
The rule is lawful because it applies to every patient equally
The rule is direct discrimination against deaf patients
The rule is harassment as it creates a hostile environment
C.why: A provision, criterion or practice that puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage triggers the s20 duty to make reasonable adjustments.

whyNot.1: Applying a rule equally can still disadvantage a disabled person and require adjustment.
whyNot.2: Direct discrimination needs less favourable treatment because of the characteristic; this is a neutral rule.
whyNot.3: Harassment needs unwanted conduct related to a characteristic; a general rule is not that.

C.q: A nurse supported a colleague's race discrimination complaint. She is then left off the training rota by her manager. What is this?
C.why: Victimisation (s27) is subjecting someone to a detriment because they did a protected act, such as supporting a discrimination complaint.

whyNot.0: Indirect discrimination is a neutral rule with a disproportionate effect.
whyNot.2: Harassment is unwanted conduct violating dignity; this is detriment for a protected act.
whyNot.3: She is not treated worse because of her own characteristic, but because of the complaint.

C.q: During handover, a nurse says an older patient's pain 'is just his age' and does not reassess it. What does this most likely reflect?
options: An assumption based on age, needing challenge
C.why: Code 1.3 requires nurses to avoid assumptions. Attributing pain to age without assessment reflects bias, which should be recognised and challenged (Annexe A 1.7).

whyNot.0: The patient has not expressed a preference; this is the nurse's assumption.
whyNot.1: Reasonable adjustments relate to disability, and not assessing pain is not an adjustment.
whyNot.2: Not assessing pain is not prioritisation; it is unsafe.

reteach.title: Ask: who, what and why
reteach.question: Faced with unfair treatment, how do you name the type quickly?

blocks.body: WHO is targeted: one person because of who they are (direct), or everyone under a rule that hits a group harder (indirect)? WHAT happened: unwanted hostile conduct (harassment) or punishment for complaining (victimisation)? WHY: is it disability-linked and could a reasonable adjustment remove the disadvantage (s20)?

blocks.text: Reasonable adjustments are owed to DISABLED people under s20. Other characteristics are protected from discrimination, but the s20 adjustment duty is about disability.

explain.body: Nine in s4. Learn them as a list and know that marriage and civil partnership is left out of the public sector equality duty.

test.q: How many protected characteristics are listed in section 4 of the Equality Act 2010?

whyNot.1: Eight is the number relevant to the public sector equality duty, not s4.

explain.body: Direct, indirect, arising from disability, harassment and victimisation, plus failure to make reasonable adjustments.

test.q: A hospital policy bans all head coverings in clinical areas, disadvantaging some patients who cover their hair for religious reasons. Which type of discrimination could this be?
test.why: A provision applied to everyone that puts people sharing a characteristic (religion or belief) at a particular disadvantage may be indirect discrimination (s19).

whyNot.1: The rule does not target people because of religion; it applies to all.
whyNot.2: No one has been punished for complaining.
whyNot.3: There is no unwanted hostile conduct directed at anyone.

explain.body: Three requirements: practices, physical features, auxiliary aids. Information in accessible formats. No charge to the disabled person.

test.q: A deaf patient needs a British Sign Language interpreter for her pre-operative assessment. Who pays?
test.why: s20(7): a person under the duty to make reasonable adjustments cannot require the disabled person to pay any of the costs of complying.

whyNot.0: The disabled person cannot be charged for the adjustment.
whyNot.2: Families cannot be required to fund the provider's duty.
whyNot.3: The duty sits with the provider, not a charity.

explain.body: Notice your own unconscious bias, challenge discriminatory behaviour calmly and promptly, support the person affected and report through local policy.

test.q: Which Code standard requires nurses to act as advocates for the vulnerable and challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour relating to their care?
test.why: Code 3.4: act as an advocate for the vulnerable, challenging poor practice and discriminatory attitudes and behaviour relating to their care.

whyNot.0: 1.5 is respecting and upholding human rights.
whyNot.2: 20.4 is keeping to the laws of the country.
